Multilevel latent profile analysis

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/lpa.Rmd
lpa.Rmd

Multilevel latent profile analysis captures heterogeneity in continuous responses by modelling variation within and across groups. Observation-level profiles describe patterns across indicators, while latent group classes capture differences in the prevalence of these profiles across groups.

In this vignette, course enrolments are nested within students. Engagement profiles describe variation in activity patterns across enrolments, while student classes capture differences in how frequently students exhibit those patterns. The profiles share the same indicator means and covariance structure across student classes, allowing their prevalence to be compared on a common basis.

Data

course_engagement has one row per course enrolment: 1,422 enrolments from 106 students. multilpa() requires a group identifier and indicator variables.

  • Group: student identifies which enrolments belong to the same student.
  • Indicators: five activity measures (browse, lectures, forum_read, forum_post, attendance), each standardized within course, so 0 is the course average.

The data are simulated, and two further variables record the structure that generated them: engagement for each enrolment and student_type for each student.

library(latents)

Clustering within groups

The descriptives() function summarizes the indicators specified in vars and their clustering within the groups specified by id. The intraclass correlation (icc) estimates the proportion of an indicator’s variance attributable to between-group differences.

descriptives(course_engagement,
             vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                      "attendance"),
             id = "student")
#>     variable    n n_missing      mean    sd   min  max n_distinct n_groups    icc
#> 1     browse 1422         0 -2.81e-05 0.989 -3.14 2.49        398      106 0.1923
#> 2   lectures 1422         0 -4.22e-05 0.989 -2.91 3.22        399      106 0.0878
#> 3 forum_read 1422         0  7.03e-05 0.989 -2.73 2.81        400      106 0.2240
#> 4 forum_post 1422         0 -2.11e-05 0.989 -2.61 3.10        397      106 0.1503
#> 5 attendance 1422         0  7.74e-05 0.989 -2.45 2.41        401      106 0.2215

Fit

The arguments n_profiles and n_group_classes specify the numbers of observation-level profiles and group classes. Estimation uses multiple expectation-maximization (EM) starts, controlled by n_starts; seed controls reproducibility. The cores argument permits parallel estimation of starts. The printed model summary includes the estimated profile means.

fit <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                         "attendance"),
                id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
fit
#> Two-level latent profile analysis: 2 profiles, 2 group classes
#> 1422 individuals in 106 groups; varying diagonal residual covariance (VVI)
#> Log likelihood: -8439.816424 | AIC: 16925.633 | BIC (groups): 16986.892
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 9 | best log likelihood reached by 10 of 10 starts (10 converged)
#> Smallest standardized Gaussian eigenvalue: 0.3715 (profiles, profile_2); Gaussian mass: 587.9; weight effective n: 606.
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 58.7% (834)   profile_2 41.3% (588)
#> Group classes group_class_1 32.5% (34)   group_class_2 67.5% (72)
#> 
#> Means
#>   indicator profile_1 profile_2
#>      browse     0.540    -0.766
#>    lectures     0.427    -0.606
#>  forum_read     0.620    -0.879
#>  forum_post     0.530    -0.753
#>  attendance     0.649    -0.921
#> 
#> Variances and standard errors: get_results(x, "profiles").
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").

The starting-value summary reports the log likelihood reached by each start. Replication of the selected likelihood provides evidence of numerical stability, although it does not establish that the global maximum has been found.

get_results(fit, "starts")
#>    start log_likelihood converged iterations error boundary
#> 1      1          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE
#> 2      2          -8440      TRUE         12  <NA>    FALSE
#> 3      3          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE
#> 4      4          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE
#> 5      5          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE
#> 6      6          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE
#> 7      7          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE
#> 8      8          -8440      TRUE         12  <NA>    FALSE
#> 9      9          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE
#> 10    10          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE

Profiles

By default, get_results() returns profile means and variances, with one row per profile and continuous indicator.

get_results(fit)
#>    profile  indicator   mean variance standard_deviation mean_standard_error
#> 1        1     browse  0.540    0.590              0.768              0.0271
#> 2        1   lectures  0.427    0.845              0.919              0.0325
#> 3        1 forum_read  0.620    0.481              0.694              0.0247
#> 4        1 forum_post  0.530    0.689              0.830              0.0295
#> 5        1 attendance  0.649    0.384              0.620              0.0223

#> 7        2   lectures -0.606    0.538              0.734              0.0309
#> 8        2 forum_read -0.879    0.363              0.603              0.0262
#> 9        2 forum_post -0.753    0.421              0.649              0.0277
#> 10       2 attendance -0.921    0.374              0.611              0.0264
#>    variance_standard_error
#> 1                   0.0295
#> 2                   0.0421
#> 3                   0.0244
#> 4                   0.0348
#> 5                   0.0196
#> 6                   0.0322
#> 7                   0.0321
#> 8                   0.0228
#> 9                   0.0261

The profile plot displays the estimated indicator means for each profile. The labels also report the profiles’ estimated shares of observations.

plot_profiles(fit)

Group classes

The "profile_probabilities" table reports the conditional probability of each observation-level profile within each group class (probability). The column group_class_probability reports the estimated proportion of groups in that class.

get_results(fit, "profile_probabilities")
#>   group_class profile probability group_class_probability
#> 1           1       1       0.170                   0.325
#> 2           1       2       0.830                   0.325
#> 3           2       1       0.786                   0.675
#> 4           2       2       0.214                   0.675

The prevalence plot compares these conditional profile probabilities, with one line per group class.

plot_prevalence(fit)

Class sizes

The "counts" table summarizes class sizes. The column effective_count sums posterior membership probabilities and can therefore be noninteger.

get_results(fit, "counts")
#>         level class effective_count effective_proportion
#> 1 individuals     1           834.1                0.587
#> 2 individuals     2           587.9                0.413
#> 3      groups     1            34.5                0.325
#> 4      groups     2            71.5                0.675

Classification

The "entropy" table summarizes classification uncertainty at both levels. For a model with more than one class, relative entropy is 1 when posterior membership is certain and 0 when every case has equal posterior probability of membership in every class. It describes separation under the fitted model, not overall model fit.

get_results(fit, "entropy")
#>         level n_classes n_units entropy_sum relative_entropy
#> 1 individuals         2    1422       60.94            0.938
#> 2      groups         2     106        4.43            0.940

The "assignments" table appends classification results to data in its original row order. The columns profile and group_class contain the most probable classes. The column uncertainty is one minus the posterior probability of the assigned profile, and the posterior_profile_ columns contain membership probabilities for each profile. The number of posterior columns depends on n_profiles. Analyses based only on the assigned labels omit this classification uncertainty.

get_results(fit, "assignments", data = course_engagement) |> head()
#>   student course sequence browse lectures forum_read forum_post attendance previous_grade
#> 1       1     23        1   0.73    -0.08       0.30       0.67       0.72           0.54
#> 2       1     19        2   0.68     0.53      -0.02      -0.55       0.70          -0.71
#> 3       1      4        3  -1.51    -0.51      -0.91      -0.80      -0.97           1.98
#> 4       1     18        4   0.64    -1.02      -1.62      -1.20      -1.26          -1.42
#> 5       1     16        5  -0.94    -0.37      -0.71      -0.28      -1.52          -0.67
#> 6       1     29        6  -0.36    -0.46      -0.77      -0.43      -1.34          -0.40
#>   engagement student_type profile group_class uncertainty posterior_profile_1 posterior_profile_2
#> 1    engaged     wavering       1           1    4.44e-04            1.00e+00            0.000444
#> 2    engaged     wavering       1           1    1.49e-02            9.85e-01            0.014854
#> 3 disengaged     wavering       2           1    2.42e-06            2.42e-06            0.999998
#> 4 disengaged     wavering       2           1    3.86e-06            3.86e-06            0.999996
#> 5 disengaged     wavering       2           1    5.75e-06            5.75e-06            0.999994
#> 6 disengaged     wavering       2           1    2.28e-05            2.28e-05            0.999977

Recovery of the known structure

For these simulated data, the truth argument permits comparison with the generating labels: engagement for profiles and student_type for group classes. Class numbers are arbitrary, so correspondence is assessed from the cross-tabulation rather than by matching numeric labels directly.

get_results(fit, "assignments", data = course_engagement,
            truth = c("engagement", "student_type"))
#>    assignment class        truth      value   n proportion
#> 1     profile     1   engagement disengaged  16     0.0274
#> 2     profile     2   engagement disengaged 569     0.9726
#> 3     profile     1   engagement    engaged 820     0.9797
#> 4     profile     2   engagement    engaged  17     0.0203
#> 5 group_class     1 student_type  committed   1     0.0161
#> 6 group_class     2 student_type  committed  61     0.9839
#> 7 group_class     1 student_type   wavering  34     0.7727
#> 8 group_class     2 student_type   wavering  10     0.2273

Reference

The calls below list the other tables, functions and views available for a fitted model. Each comment states what the call returns.

# Tables: get_results(fit, what)
get_results(fit, "all")                          # every table, as a named list
get_results(fit, "covariances")                  # within-profile residual covariances
get_results(fit, "posteriors")                   # one row per observation and profile
get_results(fit, "posteriors", format = "wide")  # one row per observation
get_results(fit, "group_posteriors")             # one row per group and group class
get_results(fit, "classification")               # class sizes and average posteriors
get_results(fit, "average_posteriors")           # mean posterior by assigned class
get_results(fit, "classification_errors")        # P(assigned class | true class)
get_results(fit, "bch_weights")                  # weights for three-step analysis
get_results(fit, "residuals")                    # residual correlations within profiles
get_results(fit, "information_criteria")         # AIC, BIC and the other criteria
get_results(fit, "model")                        # one row describing the fit
get_results(fit, "data")                         # the variables used in the fit
as.data.frame(fit)                               # the profile table

# Summaries and diagnostics
descriptives(fit)                    # indicator summaries with the ICC
descriptives(fit, by = "profile")    # the same, by assigned profile
diagnostics(fit)                     # every classification diagnostic
report(fit)                          # summary, diagnostics and plots together

# Inference and likelihood
parameter_inference(fit)             # standard errors and Wald intervals
confint(fit)                         # confidence intervals
vcov(fit)                            # covariance matrix of the estimates
logLik(fit)                          # log likelihood
AIC(fit)                             # Akaike information criterion
BIC(fit)                             # BIC with the number of groups
nobs(fit)                            # number of groups

# Plots: the plot_ functions, each with what = and "all"
plot_views()                                   # every view and what it shows
plot_profiles(fit, what = "bars")              # profile means with 95% intervals
plot_profiles(fit, what = "heatmap")           # means in standard deviations
plot_profiles(fit, what = "all")               # every profile view
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "sizes")          # effective size of each profile
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "entropy")        # per-case classification uncertainty
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "posteriors")     # posterior of each assigned profile
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "avepp")          # average posteriors, assigned by posterior class
plot(fit, what = "all")                        # every view this fit supports

# Other functions
sensitivity(fit, seeds = 1:10)       # refits under several seeds

The class enumeration article covers enumerate_classes() and get_candidate(); the latent transition analysis article covers lta(), get_tna() and get_group_tna(). The evaluation article on the package website covers bootstrap_lrt(), and the covariates article covers three_step(), r3step() and fit_staged().

Sampling weights

Sampling weights can represent unequal selection probabilities. The example below assigns twice the weight to the simulated "wavering" student class, as would be appropriate if its sampling probability were half that of the other class. The weight column is supplied through weights and must be constant within the independent sampling unit, here student. Estimation maximizes a weighted pseudo-log-likelihood after normalizing weights to sum to the number of students. The output also reports Kish’s effective sample size.

weighted_data <- transform(course_engagement,
                           survey_weight = ifelse(student_type == "wavering", 2, 1))
weighted_fit <- multilpa(weighted_data,
                         vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read",
                                  "forum_post", "attendance"),
                         id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                         weights = "survey_weight", n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
weighted_fit
#> Two-level latent profile analysis: 2 profiles, 2 group classes
#> 1422 individuals in 106 groups; varying diagonal residual covariance (VVI)
#> Sampling weights `survey_weight` (pseudo maximum likelihood): Kish effective n 94.5 of 106 units
#> Log likelihood: -8341.125778 | AIC: 16728.252 | BIC (groups): 16789.511
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 9 | best log likelihood reached by 10 of 10 starts (10 converged)
#> Smallest standardized Gaussian eigenvalue: 0.3759 (profiles, profile_2); Gaussian mass: 714.8; weight effective n: 563.8.
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 49.5% (701)   profile_2 50.5% (715)
#> Group classes group_class_1 45.2% (48)   group_class_2 54.8% (58)
#> 
#> Means
#>   indicator profile_1 profile_2
#>      browse     0.525    -0.770
#>    lectures     0.446    -0.608
#>  forum_read     0.605    -0.877
#>  forum_post     0.515    -0.742
#>  attendance     0.655    -0.921
#> 
#> Variances and standard errors: get_results(x, "profiles").
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").

For weighted fits, parameter_inference() uses sandwich standard errors by default. The package does not support vcov_type = "observed" for these fits because inverse-information standard errors do not generally represent the sampling variance under unequal weighting.

head(parameter_inference(weighted_fit), 4)
#>         level   outcome       term parameter estimate standard_error statistic   p_value p_adjusted
#> 1 measurement profile_1     browse      mean    0.525         0.0324      16.2  6.16e-59   6.16e-59
#> 2 measurement profile_1   lectures      mean    0.446         0.0367      12.2  4.54e-34   4.54e-34
#> 3 measurement profile_1 forum_read      mean    0.605         0.0264      22.9 8.01e-116  8.01e-116
#> 4 measurement profile_1 forum_post      mean    0.515         0.0319      16.2  9.48e-59   9.48e-59
#>   conf_low conf_high
#> 1    0.462     0.589
#> 2    0.374     0.518
#> 3    0.553     0.657
#> 4    0.453     0.578

The weights argument is also available in lta(), mixture_regression() and the model families fitted through multilpa(). The parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio test does not support weighted fits; its simulations do not reproduce a sampling design.

Assumptions

  • Profiles have the same means and variances in every group class.
  • Observations are independent given their group’s class, and groups are independent of one another.
  • Indicators are independent within a profile (the default diagonal covariance; covariance_model = "full" relaxes it).
  • The numbers of profiles and group classes are chosen by the analyst; see the class enumeration article for comparing them.
